title: Introduction to Short Stories
notes: A short story is a brief work of prose fiction that can normally be read in one sitting. It focuses on a single incident, character, or idea, and develops it with economy of language. Unlike a novel, a short story usually has a limited number of characters, one central conflict, and one main effect.

Plot: the sequence of events in the story — exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Character: the people (or animals, or forces) in the story; they can be round (well developed, changing) or flat (simple, unchanging). Setting: the time and place of the action, which influences mood and conflict. Theme: the central idea or message of the story — what the story means beyond its events. Point of view: the perspective from which the story is told — first person (I), second person (you), or third person (he/she/they; limited or omniscient). Conflict: the struggle at the heart of the story — internal (man vs self) or external (man vs man, man vs nature, man vs society).

A good short story starts with a hook that creates curiosity, moves through rising tension to a climax (the turning point), and ends with a resolution — which may be closed (everything is settled) or open (leaving the reader to decide). Writers often use foreshadowing (hints of what will come) and symbolism (objects or actions standing for larger ideas) to deepen meaning.
Short Stories in the NEB English Syllabus

In the NEB (Nepal Education Board) English curriculum, short stories are studied to develop skills of comprehension, analysis and interpretation. Students are expected to identify the elements above, explain the theme in their own words, relate the story to real life, and answer questions about character, setting, plot and moral values.
